source: Bertolazzi, Pezzelle, Bernardi (2026) How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
finding: Inside LLMs, validity and plausibility are each a linear direction, and the two directions point nearly the same way. This looks like one shared strength dimension, not two separate processes.
numbers: Cosine similarity of validity and plausibility vectors 0.48 to 0.64 (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B); control concepts only 0.10 to 0.13 and -0.12 to -0.17. 57 model-prompt data points; similarity predicts behavioural content effect (beta=0.557, p=0.017).
quote: both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity
limits: Open-weight Qwen models only. Syllogism set is small (10 term triples, 64 syllogism types). Authors give no proof of why the conflation arises; they guess it comes from training text where valid arguments are usually sound.
agent_relevance: Direct machine analogue of the single-dimension SDT account: one strength signal, two readouts. An agent cannot trust its own validity feel; validity must come from code or form-only restatement.

source: Bertolazzi, Pezzelle, Bernardi (2026) How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility (cross-task steering)
finding: Adding a plausibility vector flips validity judgements, and adding a validity vector flips plausibility judgements. So the two readouts share machinery causally.
numbers: Cross-task steering power is high in a subset of late layers in both directions (both models, zero-shot and CoT). Qwen3-14B, which has lower content effect, has fewer layers where steering transfers.
limits: Needs white-box access. Steering power metric is defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports treating plausibility as a contaminant of any validity check done by the same model. A black-box agent should split the two judgements across separate calls with the content removed.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) debiasing vector
finding: Subtracting the plausibility part of the validity task direction removes most content effect and can raise accuracy.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: accuracy 81.62 to 82.21, content effect 0.348 to 0.072. Qwen3-14B: accuracy 86.54 to 96.70, content effect 0.213 to 0.043 (zero-shot, scaling factor 1.5, layers 43 and 26).
limits: Best layer and scale were chosen on the same data; no held-out test seen in the text I read. Needs activation access.
agent_relevance: Shows the bias is separable in principle. For a prompt-only agent the closest copy is separate calls: one for form, one for believability, joined in code.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) prompting effect
finding: Chain-of-thought lowers content effect compared with zero-shot at the same level of validity-plausibility alignment, but the alignment itself stays equally high.
numbers: Zero-shot prompts add 0.188 content effect over CoT (p<0.001) in the mixed model; alignment does not differ by prompt style (Mann-Whitney p=0.625). Zero-shot accuracy 80.61% (Qwen3-4B) to 90.91% (Qwen3-32B); several models exceed 89% with CoT, some above 97%.
limits: Authors say they cannot yet explain why CoT helps while the representation stays entangled.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning acts like a criterion adjustment on top of an unchanged strength signal. Use it, but still check validity by code.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models and humans both say valid more often when the conclusion is believable and say invalid more often when it clashes with belief. The shift is a response bias, plotted as the proportion answering valid.
numbers: Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2 (S/M/L), Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5. Human baseline cited from Evans et al. (1983): about 90% wrongly accept invalid believable syllogisms. Wason: realistic-rule advantage in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (all z>2.2, p<0.03).
limits: Models scored by answer likelihood, not free generation. Raw scoring made several models say valid to everything.
agent_relevance: The LLM shows the same criterion shift humans show. This suggests the shift is learned from text, not from a second system.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) prompting and few-shot results
finding: A few worked examples take Chinchilla on natural language inference from heavily content-biased to near ceiling, and a plain instruction cuts bias too. On syllogisms and Wason, few-shot gives only mild gains and does not remove content effects.
numbers: Few-shot: mild accuracy gains, larger on simpler tasks, content effects remain (Appx B.2.4). Removing the instruction text did not change overall results. Instruction-tuned Flan-PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5-instruct showed no consistent drop in content effects.
limits: Exact accuracy per condition is in figures; I read only the text.
agent_relevance: Argues for one process with a controllable criterion. Task framing and examples move the criterion; they do not remove the pull of plausibility.

source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives
finding: Across 14 LLMs, most show belief bias, and accuracy on form is far higher than accuracy on natural-language believability. Better formal reasoners show smaller bias.
numbers: 12 of 14 models have positive bias; mean +10.81 points (SD 16.32; t13=2.47, p=0.028, d=0.66). Syntax accuracy 81.7% vs believability 56.2% (gap 25.5 points). Syntax accuracy vs bias size: Spearman -0.565 (p=0.035). Six models above 95%. Zero-shot CoT vs zero-shot: McNemar p=0.612. Temperature had no effect (Friedman p=0.152).
limits: Bias measured as accuracy gap between congruent and incongruent items, not with ROC or d-prime. The authors defend this because outputs are binary; it is the kind of measure Heit and Rotello criticise.
agent_relevance: Strong models separate form from belief. Weak ones do not. The gap shrinks with ability, so check the agent's own model before trusting it to judge validity unaided.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: PaLM 2 models are more logical than humans on average, yet share some human errors: sensitivity to premise order and confident wrong answers on fallacy syllogisms.
numbers: Human accuracy about 50% across the 27 syllogisms that license a conclusion other than nothing follows. The two largest models exceed human accuracy; the best is only about 75%. Zero-shot chain-of-thought used. Models rarely answered nothing follows, though it is correct for 37 of 64 types.
limits: Pretrained models only, no instruction tuning. Free-conclusion task, not a validity judgement, so no direct SDT link.
agent_relevance: Confidence is not a validity signal: the same models are most sure on the fallacies. Never use model confidence as the validity check.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Exhibit Emergent Cognitive Bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF make belief bias stronger in several model families. Few-shot examples from the same task lower it but do not remove it.
numbers: Models: GPT-3, Mistral, T5 families (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 show stronger bias). Task few-shot with fabricated words gives a noticeable drop in belief bias; format-only few-shot gives little. Mistral-Instruct belief bias drops sharply with few-shot while its certainty bias rises.
limits: I read the setup and prompting sections; exact bias scores are in figures. Small hand-written belief-bias set.
agent_relevance: Alignment training pushes the criterion toward plausible answers. Fabricated-word few-shot examples can restore a form-only criterion.

source: Ranaldi, Ranaldi, Zanzotto, Cohen (2026) Thinking in Schemas: Robust Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs (Boethius)
finding: A two-stage prompt (first name the logical form from the premises, then check validity on that form) lowers content effect and raises accuracy compared with plain, deductive and quasi-symbolic prompts.
numbers: Content effect, baseline to Boethius: Llama3-8B 73.2 to 50.7; Llama3-70B 63.5 to 49.3; GPT-4o 61.8 to 50.2; Gemma2-9B 62.8 to 56.7; Llama3-1B 76.1 to 64.9. A deductive-only prompt moved CE only a few points (GPT-4o 61.8 to 59.2). Small models needed the two stages split into separate prompts.
limits: CE stays near 50 even for the best setup. Column labels in my text extract were unclear, so only the CE column is quoted. Small models were also trained by distillation.
agent_relevance: A concrete form-first, content-later scaffold. It is the prompt-only version of the debiasing vector in c03. Good template for a validity-check slot.

source: Valentino et al. (2026) Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models Through Fine-Grained Activation Steering (AAAI)
finding: Contrastive steering controls content bias roughly linearly, but one fixed setting does not debias every model. A per-input conditional method (K-CAST) fixes some unresponsive models.
numbers: Up to 15 points formal accuracy gain on models that otherwise did not respond to steering (from search summary only).
limits: Search summary only; I did not open the paper.
agent_relevance: Same message as c01 to c03: bias is a movable offset, not a separate module.

source: Abstract Activation Spaces for Content-Invariant Reasoning in Large Language Models (2026)
finding: Models conflate plausibility with validity even when they write step-by-step explanations, so the rationale inherits the same shortcut. The paper trains small Abstractors that map content-laden activations onto the activations of the abstract (content-free) version of the same syllogism.
numbers: Paired content-laden and abstract syllogisms; Abstractors predict abstract-space representations from residual-stream states. No headline accuracy read.
limits: I read the abstract and introduction, not the results tables.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: a written rationale is not evidence of a form-only check. Content-free restatement of the argument is the cheap prompt-level equivalent.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2024) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-4 matches human property-induction judgements on most classic phenomena, with one clear failure: premise non-monotonicity. GPT-3.5 captures fewer phenomena.
numbers: Exp 1: 11 phenomena, 792 argument pairs, 110 participants after excluding 10. Exp 2: ratings of single arguments; domains mammals, birds, vehicles (24 categories each). A similarity-coverage model on human similarity ratings correlates best overall; GPT-4 nearly matches it on specific arguments. On general single-premise mammal arguments GPT-4 is uncorrelated with humans, while GPT-3.5 does better there.
limits: Humans themselves did not robustly show diversity, asymmetry and inclusion-fallacy effects in this sample. Prompt design affected results.
agent_relevance: The induction side of the subfield: models rate argument strength much like people do. An agent can use its strength ratings for ranking, but not for judging evidence that was selected.

source: Han et al. (2024) non-monotonicity failure
finding: Both models fail on non-monotonicity: adding an odd premise should lower argument strength but the models say more premises mean more strength. GPT-4's own explanations argue for monotonicity.
numbers: Example: {crow, peacock, rabbit} to bird is judged weaker by people than {crow, peacock} to bird. GPT-3.5 leaned the opposite way for general arguments; GPT-4 showed a strong opposite preference for specific arguments.
limits: Authors suggest people read premises as chosen by a helpful source and models do not model that; this is their interpretation, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Induction judgements by a model ignore how evidence was picked. An agent should record in code how each piece of evidence was collected before weighing it.

source: Cheng et al. (2024) Inductive or Deductive? Rethinking the Fundamental Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (SolverLearner)
finding: When induction is isolated (model writes the function from examples, a Python interpreter applies it), GPT-4 is perfect in every case. Deduction (applying a given rule) is where models fail, especially under counterfactual rules.
numbers: SolverLearner: accuracy 1.0 in all cases for GPT-4; mostly successful for GPT-3.5. Tasks: arithmetic in bases 8, 9, 10, 11, 16, syntactic reasoning, spatial reasoning, cipher decryption. Table 13, GPT-3.5 arithmetic: Python interpreter as executor 1.0 in all bases; GPT-3.5 as executor 0.398 (base 8), 0.196 (base 9), 0.934 (base 10), 0.152 (base 11), 0.64 (base 16).
quote: deductive reasoning presents a greater challenge than inductive reasoning for LLMs
limits: The induction target is a short program, which is easy. Counterfactual tasks may be hard because of clash with pretraining, not because of deduction as such. Authors say they do not compare the two directly.
agent_relevance: Strong support for our split: the model proposes the rule, code applies it. Moving the apply step from the model to an interpreter took base-9 addition from 0.196 to 1.0.

source: Liu, Neubig, Andreas (2024) An Incomplete Loop: Deductive, Inductive, and Abductive Reasoning in Language Models (COLM)
finding: Following a rule, learning from examples, and stating the rule are weakly linked abilities in the same model. Models can predict well without being able to say the rule, and the reverse.
numbers: Linear functions: GPT-4-turbo accuracy 96% with the true instruction vs 30% baseline. Agreement between a model's own proposed rule and its few-shot prediction accuracy is at chance level (0.0013 for GPT-3.5-turbo). Kalamang grammar sketch accuracy 27.78% (GPT-3.5-turbo), 22.22% (GPT-4-turbo), 0% (Llama-2). Vocabulary: GPT-4-turbo 87% on the easy word lug; GPT-3.5-turbo 15% on the repeat-twice term.
limits: Four models, two problem types. Reasoning types are defined by prompt form (instruction, few-shot, instruction inference).
agent_relevance: Strong dissociation on the machine side, but between rule-use and rule-statement, not between validity and plausibility. Do not accept a model's stated rule as proof it used that rule; test the rule by running it.

source: Li et al. (2025) MIRAGE: Evaluating and Explaining Inductive Reasoning Process in Language Models (ICLR)
finding: On induction tasks, models often answer new cases correctly without having induced the correct rule. They behave as neighbour-based reasoners, using nearby observed facts instead of an abstract rule.
numbers: Under the self-refine method, example-inference accuracy beats rule-induction accuracy by 16% on average. On GPT-4o, CoT-like methods cut accuracy by up to 18% and 22% on the two tasks; plain few-shot answering was best or second best in most cases.
quote: models tend to conduct correct deduction without correct inductive rules consistently
limits: Synthetic transformation rules. Main results on GPT-4o plus a few other models.
agent_relevance: A correct answer does not show the rule was right. This is G3 in machine form: pass a held-out case before trusting a rule, and prefer examples near the test case.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Induction done as: generate hypotheses, implement them as programs, check by running on observed examples, then apply to new input. This beats asking the model to predict directly.
numbers: ARC 100-problem subset (GPT-4): direct prompting 17%; programs only 23%; LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; human-written hypotheses 43%. SyGuS 94.3% with 8 programs. Natural-language intermediate without programs: 19%.
limits: Execution feedback helped little on ARC with GPT-4. Compute is high (many hypotheses and programs per task).
agent_relevance: The induction half running as a loop in an agent: propose, execute against observations, then use. Code does the deductive check. Matches our S7 and G3.

source: Parab et al. (2025) Analysis of Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search for Few-Shot Rule Induction
finding: Hypothesis search reaches human-like learning curves on 100 list functions, while direct program generation falls behind. The bottleneck is generating the right hypothesis.
numbers: Hypothesis Generator 46.4% accuracy; Summarizer 34.5%; Program Implementor 61.2%. Summarizing drops 26% of correct generator hypotheses (12.1% absolute loss). Overall test solve rate 62.0%, failure 38.1%. Implementor rescues 1092 trials (19.9% of all trials, 37.0% of double failures).
limits: List functions only, human data from Rule et al. Computation cost is high.
agent_relevance: Summary steps that prune hypotheses lose correct ones. Keep a wide hypothesis set and let execution, not the model, prune.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: The model translates the problem to logic, a solver does the deduction, and a self-refinement step uses the solver's error messages. Validity is never left to the model.
numbers: Average gain 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over CoT across five datasets. GPT-4 accuracy standard / CoT / Logic-LM: ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04; PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20 (CoT better there).
limits: Translation errors; unexecutable cases fall back to CoT. On PrOntoQA, CoT beat the solver with GPT-4.
agent_relevance: The cleanest older system that separates validity from plausibility by construction. It fits guardrail G2: revise from real solver output.

source: Cao, Tan, Akhter, Valentino, Liakata, Wang, Aletras (2026) Fundamental Reasoning Paradigms Induce Out-of-Domain Generalization in Language Models
finding: Training separately on deduction, induction and abduction trajectories over symbolic tasks transfers to realistic natural-language tasks.
numbers: Gains up to 14.60 points on out-of-domain realistic tasks (from abstract).
limits: Abstract and introduction read only. This is training, which our project does not use.
agent_relevance: Weak: it shows the paradigms can be trained apart, not that they are separate processes. Low priority for a scaffold-only build.

source: Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? An Evaluation of Parsimony in Inductive and Abductive Reasoning (2025)
finding: Models can induce hypotheses in simple worlds but produce poor-quality (not simplest) hypotheses in complex ones. Reasoning models and reasoning-oriented prompts help but do not close the gap.
numbers: Multi-hypothesis setting: accuracy of all models except GPT-4o falls from above 80% to below 50% when ontology tree height goes from 1 to 2, although the mean number of true hypotheses rises only from 3.0 to 3.5. Stronger models (GPT-5.4, o3) beat Llama3-70B. In-context demonstrations help; out-of-distribution demos do not.
limits: Synthetic first-order-logic worlds. I read the abstract, introduction and part of the results.
agent_relevance: Induction judgements need a code-checked simplicity or coverage measure, not the model's feel for which rule is best.

source: Search gap note: no LLM version of the Rips (2001) / Heit and Rotello / Stephens, Dunn, Hayes (2018) design found
finding: In searches (WebSearch, arXiv API) I found no paper that gives a model the same arguments under deduction and induction instructions and fits ROC or state-trace models. The nearest are belief-bias studies with accuracy gaps.
numbers: Searches run: LLM + induction/deduction + argument strength; LLM + signal detection + syllogisms; LLM + category-based induction; LLM + validity vs plausibility instruction framing. Zero direct hits.
limits: Absence in search is weak evidence. Papers may exist outside indexed titles.
agent_relevance: We can run this experiment cheaply: same arguments, two instruction framings, read answer probabilities as confidence, compute d-prime and criterion. An open gap.

source: Poddar et al. (2025) critique of belief-bias indices
finding: The paper repeats the human-side point that raw endorsement-rate belief-bias scores depend on baseline and that ROC curves are curved, so difference scores mislead. They then choose accuracy differences anyway for LLMs.
numbers: Cites Dube, Rotello and Heit (2010) and Heit and Rotello (2014); uses accuracy_congruent minus accuracy_incongruent.
limits: Their justification (binary outputs) skips the option of using token probabilities as a confidence rating, which would allow ROC.
agent_relevance: For our own tests, read the answer probability as a confidence rating and build a model ROC. That tests criterion shift against a real change in sensitivity.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) unitary system argument
finding: The authors argue a single transformer can show both biased and consistent behaviour depending on context, so a dual-system add-on may be unnecessary. Spending more time helps humans on Wason.
numbers: Human Wason accuracy rises with response time (z=4.44, p<0.001); slow humans reach above-chance on realistic rules.
limits: The authors state there is no mechanistic evidence yet for a conflict-arbitration process inside models. The human response-time relation is correlational.
agent_relevance: Time-on-task (more tokens) acts like the analytic criterion in people. Spend extra tokens only when a check signals conflict (G1), not on a schedule.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) prompt and sampling method
finding: The paper tried three prompting methods and settled on a generative zero-shot chain-of-thought prompt, then sampled many conclusions to build a response distribution to compare with human distributions.
numbers: Prompt: Let's think this through, step by step. 30 sampled conclusions per syllogism at temperature 0.5. Correlation of model and human response distributions fairly high, highest for PaLM 2 Small.
limits: I did not extract the mReasoner comparison numbers.
agent_relevance: Sampling a distribution over conclusions and comparing it to a theory is a usable way to find where a model follows form and where it follows habit.

source: Poddar et al. (2025) prompting strategies
finding: Prompt strategy effects were model-specific, not universal. Few-shot gave a consistent mean decline but a weak median effect; zero-shot CoT showed no change in paired counts.
numbers: Few-shot Wilcoxon p_raw=0.0195, p_adj=0.0584. ZS vs ZS-CoT McNemar p=0.612 (389 vs 374 discordant). Syntax accuracy vs consistency across content variants: Pearson r=0.877.
limits: Four prompt strategies, three temperatures, 14 models; many comparisons.
agent_relevance: Do not count on a prompt phrase alone to move the criterion. Measure per model before putting a prompt-based validity step in the schema.
